commitResults.messageTitle: Lower-case the generic user in code comments #641 (#655)
commitResults.messageBody: Address code-quality findings from the pre-release audit (beyond #556)

commitResults.messageTitle: Suggest the long option for a one-dash word
commitResults.messageBody:
Typing `--` autocorrects to an em dash in many editors and on macOS,
and pasting a command out of a document does the same. The tokenizer
folds the dashes it is handed one for one, so a pasted `--phone`
arrives as a single dash before a word, which is no option at all.
The reply says there is no -phone option and stops there, even though
`--Phone` and `-N` are each offered the option they were nearly
spelled as. Anyone whose editor rewrote the dashes is left with
nothing to go on.

Let's count the long option of a word written after one dash among
the spellings that word may stand for, so `--phone` is offered for
`-phone`, and fold case alongside the dashes so it is offered for
`-Phone` too. As before, a spelling is only offered when the command
being parsed supports it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the unreachable leading-dash guard
commitResults.messageBody:
A marker only reaches the near-spelling test from a token the
tokenizer has already read as an option, and a token is an option
only when it opens with a dash. Asking again whether the marker
opens with one is a question with a single possible answer, which
no test can make false and which invites the reader to wonder when
it might be.

Let's ask only whether the marker opens with two dashes, and say in
the comment why one dash is what is left when it does not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept adjacent hyphens in email domain labels
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB refuses an email whose domain label holds two hyphens in a row, so
an address such as student@xn--bcher-kva.de cannot be recorded. The
xn-- prefix marks an IDNA A-label (RFC 5890 2.3.2.1), which is a plain
ASCII domain of the kind the User Guide promises to accept, so a
student's real contact address is turned away.

Let's allow a run of hyphens inside a domain label and widen
VALIDATION_REGEX to match, so the hand-written checks and the regex
still agree on the same address. A label still may not be empty, nor
start or end with a hyphen.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read a modifier apostrophe as an apostrophe in names
commitResults.messageBody:
The comparison key behind name search and the possible-duplicate
warning folds the two curly quotation marks onto the straight
apostrophe and nothing else. A roster pasted into TAB carries other
characters where a reader sees an apostrophe: DʼSouza with the
modifier apostrophe, Hawaiʻi with the turned comma, Tatʹyana with the
modifier prime, and the fullwidth apostrophe and the prime that a CJK
keyboard and a spreadsheet leave behind. A TA who types D'Souza on an
ASCII keyboard is told there is no such student, and the User Guide
promises that name searches ignore apostrophe styles.

Let's read every one of them as the straight apostrophe. The grave and
the acute accent stay as they are, because both mark the letter beside
them rather than stand between two letters, which is how this key
already reads the accents it strips.

Two names that differ only in apostrophe style now also warn as
possible duplicates, which is the same promise read from the other
side. The key serves comparison alone, so no stored spelling changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the dot when a domain label is empty
commitResults.messageBody:
An address such as eve@example.com., where a full stop has been pasted
along with the address, is refused with "the last part of the domain
needs at least 2 characters". The last part the reader sees is com,
which has three, so the explanation sends them hunting for a fault
that is not there. A leading dot and a doubled dot are no better off:
they fall through to the general domain message, which never mentions
the dot at all.

Let's answer all three with one reason that names the dot, placed
ahead of the measurement of the last label so an empty tail can no
longer be mistaken for a short one. The addresses stay refused; only
the reason given for refusing them changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fit the startup error dialog on the screen
commitResults.messageBody:
The dialog that reports unreadable saved data grows to whatever height
its wrapped text asks for. A JSON syntax error has it quote the part
of the data file the failure points at, and at 1280x720 with 150%
scaling, a display the course requires us to support, that quotation
makes the dialog taller than the screen. Its heading and its Close TAB
button are then both drawn past the edge of the display, and nothing
scrolls, so neither can be brought back into view.

Let's measure the dialog against the screen it opens on, and give the
message a container that scrolls where the screen has less room than
the message asks for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the shape the whole data file must have
commitResults.messageBody:
A data file whose outermost value is not an object stops loading with
Jackson's own type error, "Can not deserialize instance of
seedu.tab.storage.JsonSerializableStudentBook out of START_ARRAY
token". Pasting just the list of students into the file is an easy
mistake to make when records are moved between files, and that message
names a storage class and a parser token instead of the one thing the
reader needs to know: the list belongs under a `students` key inside an
object.

Let's read the data file through a JsonUtil entry point that turns down
an outermost value that is not an object, with the caller's own
description of the shape its file should hold. An empty file and a file
holding only null keep the explanations they already have, neither
being a shape the caller can describe usefully.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the shape of the student list and its entries
commitResults.messageBody:
A `students` key holding an object, and an entry in that list holding a
bare name, each stop the data file loading with Jackson's own type
error: "Can not deserialize instance of java.util.ArrayList out of
START_OBJECT token", and "Can not instantiate value of type [simple
type, class seedu.tab.storage.JsonAdaptedStudent] from String value
('Bob')". Neither names the `students` field, and neither tells a
teaching assistant repairing the file that the key takes an array of
records or what a record looks like. A malformed `tags` value already
states both.

Let's read the list through a deserializer that names the field, the
offending entry and the shape each should have, as the tags
deserializer does. An entry written as null, and a field mistake
inside a well-formed record, keep the record number they report.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge upstream/master into 634-explain-a-misshapen-data-file
Keep the student index readable at the minimum width
commitResults.messageBody:
The theme holds the index column on a student card to a fixed 22
pixels, while the card itself asks for whatever width the number needs.
The theme wins. In a window at the smallest size TAB accepts, an index
of three or four digits is drawn as 9... or 1..., and nothing on the
card recovers it, not even a tooltip.

That index is what a reader types into edit, tag and delete, and the
Developer Guide asks the product to hold a thousand records, so the
command target goes missing exactly where the list is long enough to
need it. A different fixed width would only move the problem, since
the room digits take depends on their count, the font and the display
scale.

Let's drop the fixed minimum and leave the index to the preferred-size
minimum the card already sets for it. The name and contacts beside it
give up the few pixels, which is what their layout is there to do.

commitResults.messageTitle: Spell the apostrophe variants as Unicode escapes
commitResults.messageBody:
The seven characters the name comparison key reads as an apostrophe sit
in the source as themselves, and so do the two accents the tests hold
apart from them. Their glyphs are near enough identical that a reviewer
cannot tell which literal is which, nor that a list of them holds no
duplicate and no omission.

Let's write each of them as its Unicode escape, the way this file
already writes the zero-width joiner and the minus sign. The compiler
reads an escape as the character, so nothing about the comparison
changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how a pasted dash opens an option
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB reads the dashes an editor writes for a typed hyphen as the
option marker, one dash per hyphen, and the User Guide said so
until a merge resolution on the guide rewrite dropped master's
side of the conflict. No commit deletes the bullet, so nothing
points a reader at the rule, and the guide is silent on why a
pasted command behaves differently from a typed one. The
Developer Guide lost its paragraph the same way, and its parser
section still describes the suggestion as a lowercase one.

Let's say in the User Guide that a dash written for a hyphen
opens an option, that each dash stands for one `-` and a single
em dash is therefore refused with the long option suggested, and
that a dash within a value is kept. Let's record the rule for the
tokenizer in the Developer Guide, describe the suggestion as it
now stands, and give the manual testers the em dash to paste.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a manual test for a misshapen data file
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide's hand-edited data tests cover a malformed field
value and a syntax error, but not a file whose structure is the
mistake. A tester following the appendix never checks that TAB explains
a file holding only its list of students, a `students` key holding an
object, or an entry holding a bare value.

Let's add one step covering the three shapes, with the explanation each
should give.

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe the widened apostrophe fold in the DG
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide's Name row says the comparison key ignores curly
apostrophe variants, which is narrower than the key it describes: that
key also reads the fullwidth apostrophe, the prime and three modifier
letters as the straight apostrophe. A developer reading the row is told
less than the code does, and the row disagrees with the User Guide's
own promise that name searches ignore apostrophe styles.

The manual-testing appendix has the matching gap. It walks an en dash
through a search and a possible-duplicate warning, but every name in it
spells an apostrophe the one way an ASCII keyboard does, so nothing
there exercises the fold a pasted roster needs.

Let's say "apostrophe styles" in the row, the wording the User Guide
already uses, and name the accents that stay significant beside the
dash-shaped letter that already does. Let's also walk a modifier letter
apostrophe through the appendix the way the en dash is walked through
it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cap the error dialog as it is laid out
commitResults.messageBody:
The startup error dialog decides how much room its message may have
from a measurement taken before the dialog opens. It is then laid out
with its stylesheet and its fonts applied, so the height it ends up
with can differ from the one that decision was based on, and the cap
it was meant to keep to stops holding. CI reports exactly that on
macOS. A screen shorter than the dialog's own parts need has no answer
at all.

Let's work out the room left for the message each time the dialog is
measured, from the parts drawn around it in that same measurement, and
never leave the message fewer than a few lines to scroll in. Let's
also have the tests report the heights they measured, and stand aside
where the screen is too short for what they check.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge upstream/master into 626-fit-the-startup-error-dialog-on-screen
Keep the error dialog's cap to whole pixels
commitResults.messageBody:
The room the startup error dialog leaves its message is a share of the
screen's height, and on a screen whose share is not a whole number of
pixels the dialog rounds that room up as it draws it. The dialog then
stands a fraction of a pixel above the cap it is held to. CI reports
609.3 asked for and 610 drawn, on a macOS screen 677 pixels tall.

Let's take the room down to a whole pixel before the dialog is given
it, so that rounding cannot carry it past the cap, and let the test
say how far above a cap it will believe a dialog is merely rounded.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name a command that flags the student
commitResults.messageBody:
`tag 1 -a "Needs follow-up"` is refused with advice to use
`--follow-up`, and the note on `tag 1 -a "Needs_follow_up"` says the
same. `tag` takes no follow-up option, so following either message
produces a second failure that does not mention `edit` either, leaving
the user to find the right command in the User Guide.

Let's have both messages name the `edit` command that flags the student
the user just addressed, as the hint for taking the label off a flagged
student already does. `add` and `edit` take the option themselves, so
their wording stays as it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure geometry slack in device pixels
commitResults.messageBody:
The window geometry tests allow an edge to stand one logical pixel past
the area it must fit. A window's position and its size each snap to the
device-pixel grid, and an area reduced by desktop panels need not be a
whole number of device pixels, so on a 1920x1200 display at 125% the
window is rounded up twice and two tests fail on a developer's own
desktop while passing on CI and under a plain Xvfb.

Let's count the slack in device pixels instead, report the scale beside
the measurements when an assertion fails, and pin the geometry such a
display produces so the rule holds where no window manager runs to
reproduce it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Attach the slack Javadoc to the method it describes
commitResults.messageBody:
The Javadoc for the device-pixel slack helper sits above the arithmetic
regression test instead of above the helper, because the test was added
between the two. It describes a return value and a scale argument, so on
a void test method it describes nothing.

Let's put it back on snapAllowance, where the return value and the
argument it names both exist.
